verdicts.rewritten_summary: DW (late Sept/Oct 2025): Ho Chi Minh City abruptly cancelled its flagship Pride march and at least five other 2025 Pride events — HRW Asia director Patricia Gossman calls it worrying signs of a government clampdown on LGBTQ+ rights, against Vietnam's long regional-tolerance reputation; notes the 2015 lifting of the same-sex-marriage ban left unions still without legal recognition.

Outright country overview (updated Mar 2026): the law granting official transgender recognition promised for 2017 still not implemented — obstacles to gender-affirming care and legal gender-marker change persist; a recognition draft law remained under consideration as of Feb 2026. Same-sex unions were removed from the list of forbidden acts but confer no rights; LGBTIQ organisations operate openly though under government surveillance; Health Ministry declared (Aug 2022) same-sex attraction and trans identity are not mental disorders; no law against non-consensual intersex medical interventions.

Amnesty International Viet Nam 2025 report: LGBTI people's rights lacked meaningful protection in both law and practice; sits alongside wider repression — vague Penal Code arts 109/116/117/331 used to arrest at least 43 people in 2025, proposed press-law source-disclosure rules; Viet Nam re-elected to the UN Human Rights Council until 2028.

UN Viet Nam feature (30 Nov 2024): transgender women report routine discrimination at healthcare encounters ('Are you male or female? Why do you look so different to your ID card?'), heightened scrutiny, and economic/stigma-driven risk of physical and sexual violence — especially northern-province and ethnic-minority trans women; framed as case for accessible legal recognition.

Saigoneer (June 2023): Nov 2015 milestone let people who changed gender apply for civil-status change and set out legal gender recognition, but implementing guidance stalled — policy gaps persist, same-sex marriage legal but unrecognised; four trans Vietnamese describe respectful healthcare providers undone by administrative red tape.

IRB Canada Response to Information Request VNM201080.E (30 Jun 2022): Vietnamese law provides no discrimination protection on sexual-orientation or gender-identity grounds (Freedom House 3 Mar 2021); multi-source treatment briefing covering society/authorities in Hanoi and HCMC across education, employment, housing, health care.

Viet Nam News (Nov 2018): National Assembly expected to discuss a draft law protecting transgender people's legal status and rights, targeting completion by 2020 — the law never materialised; per Outright (Feb 2026) a recognition draft law was still under consideration seven years later.

Sista (Oct 2016): VPride Foundation and Vanuatu Women's Centre's first joint LGBTI human-rights workshop (SPC-funded) established that same-sex partners get no protection under the Family Protection Act 2008 and must rely on penal-code routes; USP law lecturer Anita Jowitt documented only one prosecuted violence-against-lesbians case and near-invisible LGBTI court presence; VPride (est. 2014) faced church/official/chief opposition at founding.

adds.title: Vanuatu parliament amends Marriage Act to ban same-sex marriage
adds.summary: RNZ (18 Nov 2024): Parliament amended the Marriage Act to define marriage as the union of a male and a female; Internal Affairs Minister Andrew Napuat confirmed same-sex marriages cannot be registered, and pastors must not perform ceremonies against the law.

adds.title: Vanuatu moves to ban LGBTQIA+ advocacy
adds.summary: RNZ (5 Nov 2024): Ministry of Justice and Community Services to appoint a committee drafting a national policy banning LGBTQIA+ advocacy and promotion; National Human Rights coordinator Albert Nalpini said a Council of Ministers decision earlier in 2024 targeted LGBTQIA+ activities, framing V-Pride as contrary to constitutional, Christian and Melanesian values — direct risk signal for visibly LGBT/trans visitors.

verdicts.rewritten_summary: BuzzFeed News (Jan 2018): trans women in France whose legal gender is marked male — largely those without sex-reassignment surgery — are incarcerated in all-male establishments, a documented legal grey area; example of a trans woman transferred to Lille's men's facility in 2014. Relevant as the French prison framework Wallis and Futuna inherits (French law applies unless locally overridden).

CGLPL (French national preventive mechanism) opinion of 25 May 2021 on transgender persons in places of deprivation of liberty: serious violations of fundamental rights persist in French detention, based on referrals about ~40 transgender detainees since 2010 and interviews with associations/experts; extends a 30 June 2010 opinion on trans prisoners. This French detention framework applies in Wallis and Futuna as a French collectivity.

Grokipedia compilation on transgender rights in Wallis and Futuna: French civil-law gender-marker recognition available without surgery or diagnosis since the 2016-17 French reforms; gender-identity discrimination protections since 2012 (employment, housing, services); but ~11,000 population, isolation and dominant Catholic/Polynesian norms leave practical healthcare and acceptance barriers, with fakafafine-type roles coexisting alongside stigma/concealment.

APTN (9 May 2024): Nadi, Fiji convening gathered gender-diverse community members from Samoa, Cook Islands, Vanuatu, Kiribati, Fiji, Tonga, West Papua, PNG — documents the Pacific MVPFAFF+ spectrum (fa'afafine in Samoa and American Samoa, fakaleiti in Tonga, fakafifine in Niue, etc.) as living community infrastructure Samoa participates in.

RNZ Pacific (3 May 2013): Samoa's new Crimes Act, in force that week, scrapped the crime of impersonating a woman — Samoa Fa'afafine Association president To'oto'oali'i Roger Stanley expressed relief; interview also confirms the community was not then agitating to repeal sodomy provisions, i.e. decriminalisation outcome on that front remained unchanged.

Schmidt, 'Redefining Fa'afafine: Western Discourses and the Construction of Transgenderism in Samoa' (Intersections, Aug 2001): fa'afafine = 'in the manner of a woman'; academic analysis argues fa'afafine identities are both viewed through and reshaped by Western sexuality/transgenderism discourses, with Auckland's Samoan diaspora as a contact zone — background for how visitors may encounter the term.

Outright overview (upd. Mar 2026): constitutional ban on SO discrimination (art. 24) plus the 2015 Law on Protection from Discrimination covering gender identity — but implementation inconsistent; PM Kurti's April 2024 pledge to legalise same-sex civil unions stalled, and as of Feb 2026 Parliament still failed to adopt the new Civil Code amid fierce opposition including from the ruling party.

Prishtina Insight (Jan 2019): ECtHR ruled Macedonia's surgery requirement for gender-marker change violates private-life rights (X v FYROM); Kosovo's Blert Morina — who has his own Constitutional Court case on name/gender change on Kosovo IDs — watched the ruling closely, documenting that Kosovo's legal gender recognition route ran through the courts at that time.

Prishtina Insight: third annual Pride Parade in Prishtina, with week-long exhibitions, parties, conferences and discussions by the Center for Equality and Liberty (CEL) — slogan both an appeal for tolerance and an invitation to join the parade; visible, public LGBTI organising in the capital.

Cairo 52 country review of Yemen: erosion of the rule of law plus humanitarian crisis and growing militia influence mean de-facto criminalisation is rarely enforced but is used to justify civilians taking matters into their own hands (vigilante risk); critically, the penal provisions apply ONLY in government-controlled regions — other areas sit under different factions in the ongoing conflict, so legal exposure varies by territory.

HRW report 'Audacity in Adversity' (16 Apr 2018, MENA): Yemen is one of 14 covered countries where zina provisions criminalise sex outside marriage and same-sex acts are explicitly prohibited; the report could identify NO activists in Yemen willing to speak about their work (a documented safety gap), and notes 'breach of modesty' laws used against expression.

HRW World Report 2026, Yemen chapter (events of 2025): its Sexual Orientation and Gender Identity section states Yemen's penal code prohibits same-sex relations — Article 264 punishes anal sex with 100 lashes and one year in prison if participants are not married, with the article prescribing differently if married — alongside world's-worst humanitarian crisis (19.5M needing aid) and Houthi/government factional control affecting where law applies.

Amnesty International (Feb 2024): two Huthi-run courts in Yemen sentenced more than 40 people to death, flogging or prison over same-sex conduct — the Dhamar criminal court (23 Jan) sentenced nine to death (seven by stoning, two by crucifixion) with 23 more given 6 months-10 years for 'homosexuality'/'spreading immorality', and an Ibb court (1 Feb) handed further death sentences; Amnesty demanded an immediate halt.

GayLawNet Yemen laws page: consensual same-sex sex is unlawful under Penal Code 1994 Article 264 — homosexuality between men defined as anal penetration; unmarried men punishable with 100 lashes (and up to one year's imprisonment per the statute); the canonical statute citation for Yemen's criminalisation.

IPS (16 Aug 2013) 'No Place for Gays in Yemen': Sana'a social climate — a gay man describes hiding (hood over long hair) as 'still problematic'; conservative society has no place for them while the law sees homosexuality as punishable by death; illustrates discretionary-social enforcement layered on the statutory penalty.

Full judgment, Nthabiseng Beverly Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (Gauteng High Court, delivered ~14 Nov 2025): refusal to provide gender-affirming health care to a transgender inmate for whom it was prescribed falls below the required standard of health care; refusal to allow feminising clothing/accessories likewise impugned — binding equality-court remedies for detained trans persons.

Lawyers for Human Rights case summary (14 Nov 2025): the High Court sitting as an Equality Court ruled in favour of transgender inmate Nthabiseng Mokoena against the Department of Correctional Services — orders DCS to implement accommodations, enforce its own SOPs for transgender inmates, and provide prescribed medical care.

SAHRC media statement (14 Nov 2025): welcomes the Gauteng High Court ruling in Mokoena v Head of Johannesburg Correctional Centre (Case 2024/070075) under PEPUDA — orders compelling DCS to provide gender-affirming hormone treatment at state expense and to permit clothing/cosmetics expressing her gender identity.

GroundUp (6 Aug 2025): Correctional Services has a standard operating procedure for transgender prisoners but rights organisations doubt implementation; Lawyers for Human Rights represents a trans prisoner (NM) challenging conditions — pre-echo of the Nov 2025 Equality Court win.

Outright International country overview (updated Mar 2026): Civil Union Act in force 2006; since 2003 trans/intersex people can amend sex markers under the Alteration of Sex Description and Sex Status Act (medical requirements pathologise identity; reform toward self-determination pending); 2024 Hate Crimes and Hate Speech Act explicitly protects sexual orientation, gender identity and sex characteristics; violence disproportionately hits black lesbian/trans/gender-nonconforming people in townships.

GroundUp opinion (27 Jun 2025, Mikhail Petersen): ordinary administrative tasks are fraught with risk for trans people — medical requirements under the Alteration Act lock people out of legal gender recognition, binary sex classification excludes non-binary people; Gender Dynamix's 2024 report documents a trans woman denied filing a domestic-violence case after showing her ID (police mockery).

MambaOnline (6 Jan 2025): 23-year-old trans woman Aobakwe Mahlobo (make-up artist, Soshanguve→Winterveld) survived an unprovoked hate-crime assault at a Tshwane tavern on 26 Dec 2024, left with severe facial injuries and physical/emotional scars — she spoke out publicly; illustrates violent hate-crime risk against visible trans women in social venues.

OUT LGBT Well-being rights watch (Dec 2024): East London activists spotlighted trans healthcare access — memorandum to Frere Hospital over year-long treatment delays; escalating hate violence with five LGBTQIA+ murders reported; also covers the Tshwane tavern attack (arrest made).

Academic article (PER/PELJ 2024) 'Did the CPA Shut the Bathroom Door?': analyses whether gender-segregated bathrooms to the exclusion of transgender/non-binary persons constitute unfair discrimination under CPA s9 read with Constitution s9 — argues trans people do not in practice experience equal protection in facility access; relevant to visitor facility anxiety.

Daily Maverick opinion (19 Jan 2026, Mikhail Petersen/Gender Dynamix): makes the legal gender recognition case — mismatched documents expose trans people to humiliation, denial of service and even arrest threats for 'fraud'; defines LGR as changing marker/name on official documents to align with identity; argues recognition should be a right grounded in dignity.

IOL/SAPA: Justice Minister Jeff Radebe launched a programme against gender-based and LGBTI violence, citing the Constitution's equality clause — early (2010s-era) government recognition of LGBTI violence as a policy problem; historic context for the later Hate Crimes Act (2024).

Amnesty International campaign story (26 Nov 2024) 'Madalitso's story': a Zambian medical professional —36, three years behind bars by Nov 2024 — imprisoned for consensual same-sex conduct; his medical expertise lost to a health system short of workers; frames individual persecution of LGBTI people in Zambia.

US State Dept 2021 Country Report, Zambia: government continued to reject recognition/protection of LGBTQI+ rights; police perpetrated violence and verbal/physical harassment based on gender identity and sexual orientation; LGBTQI+ people at risk of societal violence from prevailing prejudice and misperceptions of law; advocacy groups report police routinely solicit bribes after arresting LGBTQI+ individuals (fines reportedly raised from 500 to 15,000 kwacha / $30-$900); discrimination in employment, housing, education and health continued.

HRW report 'Dignity Debased' (12 Jul 2016): documents forced anal examinations in at least eight countries including ZAMBIA — less frequent there than Egypt/Tunisia but prosecutors have introduced medical reports from anal exams as court evidence in sodomy cases (incl. a mass trial of ~20 men); recommends worldwide ban; such exams are treated by victims as painful, degrading sexual violence.

US State Dept 2022 Country Report, Zambia: no credible efforts to rescind discriminatory laws targeting LGBTQI+ persons; when police detain LGBTQI+ members they often threaten charges under other laws to extort bribes for release; no credible reports of government agents condoning violence, but President Hichilema's 30 May statement opposing basic LGBTQI+ protections and same-sex marriage produced a spike in public hate speech, threats and assaults; societal violence and employment/housing/education/health discrimination continued.
